# R7 — Justification

Every semantic unit of `library/core/rules/R7-diverge-before-converge.md`, why it is there, what fails without it, and where it comes from. Sources are the nine repositories in `SOURCES.md` and the blueprint sections named by ID.

| # | Unit | Why it exists | What breaks if removed | Source / inspiration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title and ID `R7 — Diverge before converge` | The ID is the handle other documents cite; the title states the ordering in four words. | Other docs cite an unnamed rule; "diverge" alone reads as brainstorming, and "before converge" is the actual constraint. | Blueprint R7; BMAD `converge.md` |
| 2 | Trigger list: concept, core loop, mechanic, level, visual direction, player-facing name | Bounds the rule to choices that have alternatives; excludes tuning numbers, bug fixes and code identifiers. | Without a list the rule either swallows every decision (divergence for a jump height or a variable rename) or is read as concept-only, so levels and names skip it. | Blueprint R7; godot-proposals problem framing |
| 3 | "judgment begins only after the set is closed" | The invariant: the critic's start time, not the number of ideas, is what the rule protects. | The critic runs inside generation, kills variant 3, and the set becomes the first idea plus decoration. | BMAD: "Never run convergence while ideas are still flowing" |
| 4 | Why: the first idea is the most available; later work defends an uncompared choice | Gives the mechanism (availability plus post-hoc rationalization), so the rule is not obeyed as ritual. | The rule reads as taste and is skipped when the first idea feels strong — which is exactly when it binds. | BMAD: "premature judgment is what kills good ideas"; Bevy: "relative consensus" |
| 5 | At least 20 variations | A floor past the obvious five to seven; forces recombination instead of listing. | Sets of five are the first ideas ranked; no variant from outside the obvious cluster appears. | BMAD: "Aim past 100 ideas"; S06's twenty |
| 6 | "written down" | External memory; makes the set inspectable by A04 and reusable at the next choice. | The set exists only in the head; memory keeps the winner and forgets the range; A04 has nothing to check. | BMAD memlog; rust-lang/rfcs "Alternatives" field |
| 7 | Three bad or absurd variants | They mark the edge and often hold the fragment that survives; licensed badness lowers the cost of a weak idea. | The set clusters around "reasonable"; range collapses; the surprising fragment is never written. | BMAD: "resist concluding"; Cataclysm: "unexpected inversions of gaming tropes" |
| 8 | No critique during generation: no score, no "but", no backlog entry | Keeps the phases apart in small acts; each of the three is a convergence move in disguise. | Scoring or a backlog line during generation ranks ideas before the set exists, and the generator self-censors. | BMAD divergence/convergence separation |
| 9 | The critic (A04) speaks only after the set is closed | Gives the critic a phase and a job; stops it becoming a co-generator or a blocker. | Either no criticism at all, or critique arrives at variant 2 and ends the search. | Blueprint A04; BMAD: "deliberate opposite phase" |
| 10 | Distant references: film, music, architecture, nature | These import structure and feeling without importing a genre's solved answers. | References default to the last game played; the set becomes genre variants. | rust-lang/rfcs "Prior art"; Cataclysm: "if it works in reality" |
| 11 | "only after that compare with games" | Games are the most contaminating reference: they arrive with a genre, a control scheme and an audience. | The genre template is imported before the problem is understood; divergence collapses into "like X but". | BMAD genre trap; Bevy vision statement, rejected as a substitute for options |
| 12 | "A game reference imports its genre; a film reference imports a feeling" | States why the order matters in one memorable line; without a reason the order is dropped under time pressure. | The ordering looks arbitrary and gets reversed; distant references become decoration. | Cataclysm reality tenet; rust-lang/rfcs prior art |
| 13 | `spark` pass: 10 variants, cheap and unranked | A second, lower-cost pass after the set is nominally complete; unranked so it cannot become a shortlist. | The first 20 settle into a shortlist; later variants are only elaborations of the leaders. | superpowers: "a spike … to feel things out" |
| 14 | "S06 runs this; R7 is why it is not optional" | Draws the boundary: procedure versus principle; prevents two diverging procedures. | R7 grows into a second brainstorm procedure that drifts from S06, and the two disagree on number and order. | Blueprint S06; rubric integration criterion |
| 15 | Tinker budget: 10–15% of creative time | Protected slack where nobody asks a question; bounded so it cannot eat production. | Exploration happens only in leftover time — that is, never; or it becomes unbounded and the sprint dies. | Bevy: "Rapid experimentation over API stability" |
| 16 | Exclusions: questions (R2), verdicts, backlog entries | Defines the space by what must not enter it; a tinker block with a question is a review. | The block becomes a question session or a task list; the unasked space never opens. | R2; BMAD: "never let it leak into a generating batch" |
| 17 | Output: an artifact and one line, "what surprised me" | Makes the block observable without paperwork; an artifact is checkable, a feeling is not. | "I explored" is unfalsifiable; the block is cut first when time is short. | BMAD: "The best sessions end with the user surprised" |
| 18 | "An empty line is a result" | Removes the incentive to invent a surprise; records a real outcome. | Every block produces a fake insight; the log becomes noise and stops being read. | BMAD memlog honesty; project logic |
| 19 | "Ten percent of a week is half a day: put it on the calendar" | Converts a percentage into a schedulable block. | Ten percent stays a number nobody allocates; the budget exists on paper only. | Bevy protected experimentation; D03/D05 separation |
| 20 | "Alive but illegible" | Names the state gates currently kill: clearly there, not yet explainable. | Unexplainable-but-real ideas die at the gate; only pre-articulated ideas survive. | Cataclysm lore adjusted for a great idea; KEP staged graduation |
| 21 | One extension at G1 | Bounded exception, matching G1's "extend once"; one is enough to test, few enough to end. | No extension kills live ideas; unlimited extension produces concepts that never resolve. | Blueprint G1; KEP graduation criteria |
| 22 | "kill only when nothing is there, not because the answer is unclean in 48 hours" | Ties the kill to substance, not to eloquence or a deadline. | Kill depends on how fast the developer can explain, which punishes exactly the new ideas. | Cataclysm: "adjust the details … to make room"; KEP early stage |
| 23 | "An extension is a dated decision, not a delay" | Stops the extension becoming an indefinite reprieve; links it to the gate's one-line plus date. | The concept sits in limbo; nobody can say when it was extended or why. | Blueprint G1 and D03; KEP graduation |
| 24 | Record the doubt beside the concept | The illegible part is the reason for the extension; without it the next review starts from zero. | The extension looks arbitrary at the next gate; the doubt is re-litigated or forgotten. | BMAD memlog; MADR "Considered Options" |
| 25 | G2 counts links, not systems | Measures interaction density, which produces emergence, instead of breadth. | Slice reviews reward system count; ten shallow systems pass and nothing interacts. | Cataclysm: "huge number of ways"; blueprint G2 |
| 26 | Link = one system reading or writing another's state | Makes "ten links" countable and blocks counting UI touches or shared config as links. | The number inflates; two systems joined by a shared enum look integrated. | Cataclysm gameplay doc; project logic |
| 27 | "three systems with ten links beat ten systems without" | A concrete trade-off a gate can apply without a formula. | The principle stays abstract; the gate defaults to counting features. | Cataclysm; blueprint G2 |
| 28 | "Emergence is where surprises come from (S08)" | Connects the interaction budget to the surprise goal and to prototype practice. | The budget reads as architecture taste; the link to divergence is lost. | Blueprint S08; Cataclysm |
| 29 | "Write the surprising result in the S06 brief, not only the winner" | Divergence's product is the unexpected; the winner is already in the decision record, and the brief is the artifact both S06 and the next choice read. | The set is reduced to its winner; the fragment no variant predicted is lost, or is written where nobody looks. | MADR "Considered Options"; BMAD surprise; S06 brief |
| 30 | "what appeared that no variant predicted" | Operational definition of "surprising", applied while the brief is written. | "Surprising" degrades to "slightly new"; the brief fills with the expected. | BMAD: "user surprised by what came out" |
| 31 | "the asset the next choice inherits" | Reason to keep the line in the brief: it seeds the next set. | The brief becomes a museum; nobody reads it before the next choice. | BMAD memlog; rust-lang/rfcs "Unresolved questions" |
| 32 | Check: S06 produces, A04 checks closure, G1 and G2 apply the budgets | Assigns each check to an existing artifact; no new ceremony. | The rule has no enforcement point; A04 approves sets that were never closed. | Blueprint A04, G1, G2 |
| 33 | Evidence list: 20 variants, a spark pass, one surprise line per tinker block | A manual checklist A04 can apply without interpreting intent. | "Check" stays vague; the reviewer judges by feel. | Rubric testability; project logic |

## Deliberate omissions

| Omitted | Reason |
|---|---|
| The procedure for generating the twenty (prompts, techniques, timing) | S06 owns it; a second procedure inside a rule drifts and the two eventually disagree. |
| Question batching, "you decide", no-repeat rules | R2 owns questions; R7 only names R2 as an exclusion from tinker time. |
| A scoring or ranking method for the critic | A04 owns the critic; a method here would bind it and turn the rule into a rubric. |
| Gate verdict vocabulary and thresholds | G1 and G2 own their decisions; R7 adds two budgets, not a new verdict. |
| A template for the set or the spark pass | S06's one-page brief is the format; a second template competes with it. |
| Hour logs for the tinker budget | A solo developer will not keep timesheets; the artifact and the calendar block are the evidence instead. |
| A taxonomy of "distant" (how far is far) | Examples carry it; a taxonomy invites category debates instead of work. |
| Named game examples | They date fast and import exactly the genre reference the rule warns about. |
| Engine, OS or editor mechanics | Core rules must not contain them; they would break portability across projects. |
| A new eval ID | The blueprint assigns R7 no eval; the check routes through S06, A04, G1 and G2. |
| Advice on persuading a stakeholder to allow divergence | That is negotiation, covered by R2's question budget, not a design rule. |
| A time-box such as one hour for twenty variants | The count is the box; a clock pushes toward fast, shallow variants. |
| Anti-pattern names (pet idea, highest-paid person) | The no-critique rule already blocks the mechanism; the names add jargon without a check. |
